identity_evidence.quote: A 12-year-old male patient, born at term with no history of disease, drug use, or surgery, was referred to the pediatric neurology department for investigations and follow-up after two epileptic episodes. The patient was admitted and observed for two weeks, and medication was prescribed. Electroencephalography, brain, cervical, and thoracic magnetic resonance imaging, and blood tests were performed. No pathology was observed in the imaging or blood test results. However, during follow-up, mirror movements in the upper extremities were noted. The patient was referred to the physical medicine and rehabilitation department for the recommended rehabilitation. Written informed consent was obtained during the patient’s consultation and before the video recordings from the patient’s parents. The patient and family were informed that all recordings taken from the case would be used for medical and academic information purposes, with personal information kept confidential.

evidence.quote: The patient was informed of the diagnosis, and a rehabilitation plan was implemented (Table 1). As per the literature, the patient was started on hand-arm bimanual intensive therapy including the lower extremity (HABIT-ILE), which involved both upper and lower extremities. The HABIT-ILE has been successfully used in children with cerebral palsy. For our patient, one-to-one HABIT-ILE was planned for 50 h in 20 days. The patient’s mother was instructed on the at-home exercise program to be performed and the arrangements that could be made in daily life. The patient was followed up regularly once a week. At the three-month follow-up, significant improvements in the upper extremity mirror movements was observed. Consequently, follow-up was adjusted to monthly.

Mirror movement disorder is defined as the involuntary involvement of contralateral homologous muscles during voluntary movements, and its rehabilitation is a labor-intensive process. In this case report, we described a 12-year-old male patient with epilepsy who developed mirror movements in the upper extremities. The patient underwent hand-arm bimanual intensive therapy including the lower extremity for 20 days and 50 h. The Woods-Teuber evaluation score, which was high before treatment, was lower after treatment. During the three-month follow-up, the patient’s condition continued to improve.

events.description: Post-treatment bilateral mirror scores improved to 3

evidence.quote: The Woods-Teuber scale was applied to rate mirror movements. The patient was asked to perform three basic movements. These were (i) repetitive tapping of the index finger on the thumb, (ii) alternating supination and pronation of the hand, and (iii) repetitive alternating touching of each fingertip. Afterward, variants of the tasks were administered (e.g., fist opening, clenching, and finger tapping on a table). While the patient was performing these movements, the movements in the other hand were scored as (0) no clear imitative movements, (1) barely discernible repetitive movements, (2) slight mirror movements or stronger but briefer, repetitive movements, (3) strong and sustained repetitive movements, and (4) movements equal to those observed in the active hand.[] The patient’s right hand was dominant. Before treatment, the left hand scored 9 points during right-sided movements, and the right hand scored 12 points during left-sided movements. After 50 h of the rehabilitation program, when the same evaluation was performed, both sides scored 3 points. At the three-month evaluation, both hands scored 3 points. The patient’s evaluations, before and after treatment, were video recorded. (Video 1, Video 2).

events.description: Post-treatment bilateral mirror scores improved to 3

evidence.quote: The Woods-Teuber scale was applied to rate mirror movements. The patient was asked to perform three basic movements. These were (i) repetitive tapping of the index finger on the thumb, (ii) alternating supination and pronation of the hand, and (iii) repetitive alternating touching of each fingertip. Afterward, variants of the tasks were administered (e.g., fist opening, clenching, and finger tapping on a table). While the patient was performing these movements, the movements in the other hand were scored as (0) no clear imitative movements, (1) barely discernible repetitive movements, (2) slight mirror movements or stronger but briefer, repetitive movements, (3) strong and sustained repetitive movements, and (4) movements equal to those observed in the active hand.[] The patient’s right hand was dominant. Before treatment, the left hand scored 9 points during right-sided movements, and the right hand scored 12 points during left-sided movements. After 50 h of the rehabilitation program, when the same evaluation was performed, both sides scored 3 points. At the three-month evaluation, both hands scored 3 points. The patient’s evaluations, before and after treatment, were video recorded. (Video 1, Video 2).
